title: Potassium iodide (KI): what it can and can’t do
summary: Potassium iodide (KI) protects only the thyroid, and only from radioactive iodine. CDC says it will not help in a nuclear bomb emergency: fallout is the danger, and getting inside is the protection. Take it only if public health or emergency officials or a healthcare provider tell you to. This app gives no dose.
doFirst: Get inside, stay inside, stay tuned: that is always the best protection in a radiation emergency (CDC).
Don’t leave your shelter to look for KI. Going out for it could expose you and your family to dangerous radiation (CDC).
Take KI only if public health or emergency officials or a healthcare provider tell you to (CDC).
Don’t use table salt or foods with iodine instead: they don’t help. Iodine supplements may not work and can hurt you (CDC).

list: KI is a form of iodine that is not radioactive. Taken at the right time, it fills the thyroid, a gland in the neck, so there is no room left for radioactive iodine (CDC).
It protects only the thyroid, not any other part of the body (CDC).
It protects only against radioactive iodine, not against other radioactive materials (CDC). FDA: it is not a general protection against radiation.
It works best taken shortly before or right after radioactive iodine gets into the body (CDC).
It may not give the thyroid full protection, and it is not a treatment: it can’t undo damage already done (CDC).

blocks.warn: CDC: KI will not help in a nuclear bomb emergency. Radiation from fallout is the biggest threat to your health after a nuclear explosion.

list: Fallout is made up of hundreds of kinds of radioactive material. There is relatively little radioactive iodine in it compared with the others, which can harm you from outside your body (CDC).
KI would not protect you from any of the radioactive materials in fallout except radioactive iodine (CDC).
If you were somewhere you could take in enough radioactive iodine for KI to help, you would already have been exposed to deadly levels of radiation from fallout outside your body (CDC).
Relying on KI can make you think you are protected when you are not (CDC).

blocks.label: Fallout warning: what to do first

blocks.p: CDC: taking KI after a dirty bomb would probably not help, and KI can be dangerous to some people.

sections.h: When officials might call for it

list: Radioactive iodine is most common in nuclear power plant accidents. Most radiation emergencies involve other radioactive materials, not radioactive iodine alone (CDC).
In normal times in New York, after a nuclear power plant emergency, local or state health officials announce when to start taking KI and when to stop (New York State Department of Health).
After a radiological or nuclear event in the United States, local public health or emergency officials will tell the public whether KI is needed (FDA).

blocks.p: Nuclear power plant accidents are not covered in this app yet.
If officials call for KI, this is who CDC says it is meant for. It is never a reason to take KI without being told to.

list: CDC recommends KI only for people under 40, and for women who are pregnant or breastfeeding. Younger people’s cells are growing faster, which puts them at risk of thyroid cancer after breathing in radioactive iodine (CDC).
Newborns under 1 month old have the highest risk of thyroid cancer from radioactive iodine (CDC).
Adults over 40 have a much lower risk of thyroid cancer and are more likely to have health problems that KI can make worse. They take KI only if officials recommend it (CDC).
People with certain medical conditions, including known iodine sensitivity, should not take KI, or should ask a healthcare provider first (CDC).
FDA: people with known iodine sensitivity should avoid KI, and so should people with dermatitis herpetiformis or hypocomplementemic vasculitis, two very rare conditions.
FDA: people with nodular thyroid with heart disease should not take KI. People with multinodular goiter, Graves’ disease or autoimmune thyroiditis should be treated with caution.
A seafood or shellfish allergy does not necessarily mean you are allergic to iodine (FDA).
Not sure? Ask a healthcare provider (FDA).
KI can cause stomach upset, rashes, swollen salivary glands and allergic reactions (CDC).
Severe shortness of breath after taking it needs medical care at once (FDA).
Taking more than you are told to, or more often, gives no more protection and can cause severe illness or death (FDA, CDC).
More than a single dose may cause later problems with normal development, and newborns under 1 month old who get more than one dose can develop an underactive thyroid (CDC).
Table salt and foods that contain iodine: they don’t prevent radioactive material getting into the body, and eating large amounts could be harmful (CDC).
Dietary supplements that contain iodine: they may not protect the thyroid and can hurt you (CDC).
Drinking iodine: FEMA’s planning guidance treats posts urging people to drink iodine to protect themselves from radiation as a rumor for officials to confront.
Use only KI products approved by the FDA (CDC).
KI is sold without a prescription (FDA). Only products approved by the FDA should be used (CDC).
This app gives no dose. If officials or a healthcare provider tell you to take KI, use it only as directed (CDC).
Keeping KI is never a reason to go outside, delay getting inside, or leave shelter (CDC).
